utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 30th of March. I would like to greet the witness, Mr. Vidovic, as well as all the accused that are in the courtroom and those that are not in the courtroom. I would like to greet the counsels, all the members of the OTP who are in the courtroom, as well as everybody else assisting us in the courtroom. We are going to proceed with the examination-in-chief. We have 34 minutes left. Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, and everybody else in the courtroom. I'd like to apologise to everybody for skipping some documents yesterday, so we're going to go through them today, and perhaps we'll need a little time to find the documents I wish to address. We looked at 5D04350 yesterday. And after that, we're going to skip -- having looked at that, we're going to skip six documents and go to 5D02146.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vidovic, you told us yesterday that you and the other members of your department were involved up at the front-line, that you held the line at the Bulevar. Can you tell us now whether that had any effect on your work?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly did affect our work as a service.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Have you managed to find the document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a special report signed by you, sent to Mr. Coric, and in the report, in the first sentence, it says that: "From Mr. Josip Djogic, we have learned about the decision on the order of Mr. Rade Lavric that employees and operatives of the Mostar Centre should go to the front defence line confronting -- facing the enemy." Do you remember this, and can you tell us what type of decision it is, what type of order it is, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision made by the operative zone, that is to say, ordering us to go up to the front-line. And we were against that, but through our battalion we said that we had to respect the decision taken by the operative zone, although we challenged it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you look at the next document now, please, the very next one, P05471. This is a document signed by Mr. Coric. It is about the engagement of the police up at the front-line. And in paragraph 3 from the end of the document, on the last page, it says the following: "Terror and crime of all types is on the increase, and that is worrying, and threatens to lead to anarchy and lawlessness in the free territories. "I claim with responsibility that we are not able to perform even regular military police tasks with the forces remaining after the deployment of the military police on front-lines, not to mention complex interventions and other significant military police tasks." Tell me, please, do you agree with Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I said earlier on. Based on the previous document, we were already up at the front-line, we were already on our way. Instead of our military police tasks, regular ones, we were already moving towards the front-line, so this is precisely what I was saying earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to skip quite a few documents and move towards the end of the binder to document P03651. It's towards the end. You told us yesterday -- P03651. You told us yesterday that you went to Heliodrom because there were detainees there whom you either kept there for police processing or the investigative judge had ordered them a period of detention while the investigation was ongoing. Now, this is a document signed by you, and I'm going to read certain sections of it and then I'm going to ask you some questions about it. The document is titled "Decisions Adopted at the Meeting Held in Ljubuski on the 22nd of July, 1993, at the Military Police Administration." In the document, you go on to say: "With regard to the meeting held on the 22nd of July, 1993, in Ljubuski, at which, in addition to the chief of the Military Police Administration of the HZ-HB, Mr. Valentin Coric, all department chiefs in the Military Police Administration were present, and we would like to inform you of the following for the sake of clearer co-operation in future: "The activities and competence of the Crime Prevention Department were reiterated once more at the meeting. It was assessed that direct co-operation with the active police (military police and MUP) and the District Military Court was good, the initiation of proceedings was clear and there was no overlap, while our co-operation with officers of the Central Military Remand Prison must be indirect. Immediacy is achieved through the District Military Court. We conduct criminal processing until we assess that there are elements to move criminal proceedings and the SIS co-operation is necessary. Therefore, all the individuals who are detained and against whom no criminal proceedings have been initiated or no criminal report has been filed, pursuant to the chief of the Military Police Administration, are unknown to our department. This refers solely to the large number of Muslims who were brought indiscriminately to the Central Military Remand Prison building and then forgotten. Through inertia, the Crime Prevention Department conducted interviews with over 2.000 people, but not a single one of them was of any interest with respect to crime. The question was posed. Mr. Coric was asked about the duties -- about our duties and was the reason for him issuing the order for us to start dealing with crime." Tell me, please -- in the first paragraph you state that: "In order to ensure clearer future co-operation, we should like to inform you of the following:" Who is it that you are informing by compiling and sending this document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm writing this document to the head of the Military Remand Prison at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to tell me now, with respect to the third paragraph, the problem of interviews with over 2.000 people were mentioned. Do you remember what interviews these were?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in July 1993, through our military police battalion, we received an order telling us to report to Heliodrom and that we should make a list there of all the detainees who had been disarmed of the HVO who were Muslims and whose units had isolated them and put them in Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you pause there for a moment. Let me just ask you, you said it came in through the battalion. Was the order issued to you by the battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion received the order via the operative zone, and it just forwarded it on to me -- to us based on some hierarchy or chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You said that you made a list, drew up a list. What kind of list was that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the premises of the Military Remand Prison of Heliodrom, we took down the basic details of the persons there; names, surname, and where they were from, just the basics. And we did that together with the MUP and SIS and some workers from the Heliodrom Prison itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember the name of the person from SIS who did this job with you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as SIS is concerned, it was the SIS of the brigade; that is to say, Mr. Ivica Pusic was mostly present when we worked together with SIS.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when those lists were compiled, did you take them with you, did you hand them over to someone? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those lists were handed over, through the warden of the prison, to the Centre for Social Work and for Displaced Persons. There was a woman called Biljana Nikic, I remember, and we actually compiled those lists for her. And I state very precisely here that those lists weren't of any interest to us with respect to crime-solving.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's go back two documents. P05128 is the document I'd like us to look at now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Mr. Vidovic, the document that we've just seen, P03651, is an important document. We see that you drew up a list of 2.000 people, and it seems that according to you, those people had no connection with the crimes in question. Should we infer from that that they should have been freed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't decide about that, but I was given a task to do which I didn't feel I ought to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you were given this task, and it's to your credit, but who was in a position to free those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I didn't know under whose authority they were or who had the authority to do that, because they were just disarmed members of the Croatian Defence Council and their direct, immediate commanders had authority over them. I only knew things up to that level. And I was only interested in the people I worked with in the Crime Department, so this task prevented me from going about my daily duties and carrying those out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Among those 2.000 people that were interviewed, were they all soldiers from the HVO or were there, amongst those, civilians as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ones that I interviewed and whose details I took down, they were HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity in the vast majority of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying "in the vast majority of cases." Why? Were there also HVO soldiers that were not of Muslim ethnicity that were also detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't remember exactly now, but I assume there were cases like that too. But I have to mention that we're dealing with July 1993 here. That's the period.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We said we'd move on and go to P05128.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a document signed by the lady you mentioned a moment ago, Biljana Nikic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: The document number is P05128. I misspoke and said "go forward two documents," but you need to go back two documents. This is a document, as I was saying, signed by Biljana Nikic, whom you mentioned earlier on. You can take a look at it. We see that it was sent to the Crime Investigation Department, Mostar, among others. Do you recognise the document? Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it's about?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Biljana Nikic is contacting our department and asking us, from the aspects of crime investigation, to check the criminal responsibility of these two persons, Ifet Selimovic and Ibro Maric, and it's sent to the Crime Investigation Department of Mostar, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: When you say to check out the criminal responsibility, does that mean that you're checking your records to see if they have a criminal record?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document immediately after that one, which is P05371. This is a certificate, stating your name, but it says that it is your name; however, somebody else signed it. And it says here that there are no disciplinary or criminal proceedings instituted against the persons on this list. Tell me, what kind of a certificate is this? Is that the one that you spoke of a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely an answer to the questions that were put to us by the Office for Refugees and [indiscernible]. I see that someone else signed this, Damir Cipra, I think. That is my colleague from the office; however, that is of lesser importance. This is exactly the way we issued these certificates, as to the request of the office. That is to say, once we check that certain persons, from the request that they had sent us, and when we are sure that there are no criminal proceedings against these persons, then we issue such a certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to make an observation on the translation. Here, in the English text, at least, one speaks of criminal or misdemeanor proceedings, and the translation for "misdemeanor" was "disciplinary," but that is wrong. "Misdemeanor" is minor crimes, but it is clearly not disciplinary. And as we are in the field of the military, I think it's important to make sure that the distinction is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to move three documents back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Witness, the question of translation is important. Could you perhaps read, in your own language, what it says when the you hereby certify that those people have not been subjected to any proceedings? Could you please read that in your own language, please, because I want to be sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Certificate." Your Honour, you want this document, 3371, P371 [as interpreted]; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is P03571, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Certificate": "It is hereby certified that this centre is not conducting criminal or misdemeanor proceedings against the persons from the above-mentioned list and request submitted by your office. It is issued for the purpose of regulating release from the Mostar SVIZ and for travel abroad, as follows:"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let us just explain in order to avoid any kind of misunderstanding. You heard what His Honour said a few moments ago. Misdemeanors are minor crimes that a misdemeanors court deals with. It is not disciplinary violations that are meant by that; right? You're nodding, but you have to give a verbal answer.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Misdemeanors are, for example, disrupting public law and order, drunken driving, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to go back a few documents, three documents to be precise, so we're going back to 5D032 -- 4226, rather, 04226. It consists of several pages. On the first page, there is a reply to a request, and on the remaining few pages there are bulletins for wanted persons. These are documents sent to the District Military Court, and it says: "In response to your requests, we are forwarding wanted notices for the following persons:" Can you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has to do with a request from the District Military Court that asked us to submit to them the bulletins that we issued for certain persons who were wanted because criminal proceedings had been initiated against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now I see that we are -- you are submitting these documents. Do you know what the Military Court does with them afterwards? Do they submit these bulletins to someone or what?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the domain of their authority, they submit these documents to check-points on roads and also to commanders of the units that these persons may come from, and also to border-crossing points; that is to say, all locations that could be relevant for the possible arrest of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the document before that, 5D02040, please. This is the record of an interview, and it shows that you were interviewing a person on the premises of the Heliodrom, and the person's name is Alija Lizdo. Tell me, how did that come about? How come you were interviewing this gentleman? Were you processing him, or is there some other reason for that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We co-operated with the SIS all the time, and we received information from them that at the Heliodrom, to the best of their knowledge, there was a person who was of interest to us. My colleague, Toni Ramljak, and I went to interview the mentioned gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you say that he was of interest to you, that means that he could have some knowledge of certain crimes or perhaps that he was responsible, himself?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so that ultimately we may issue -- or, rather, file a criminal report against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this person was of interest to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We interviewed the mentioned person, and we did not find any elements related to a crime. I would just like to add here that by then I had already known Mr. Alija Lizdo as a journalist. To this day, I'm on very good terms with him. I see him very often. That is the only thing I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after you realised that he was not of interest to you, did you have any authority over that person after that, once you realised that he was of no interest to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our only job was to compile a record of that interview and to send it to the mentioned -- or, rather, to take it to the mentioned gentleman so that he could read it and sign it in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Did you provide information to that effect, that he was of no interest to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through the daily report we referred to our work with that person, and we said whether he was or was not of interest to us, from the point of view of the Crime Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to skip a few more documents, and we're going to advance six documents, as it were. P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand why this journalist was being detained. I can see that he was part of the ABiH since May 1992, that he was in charge of propaganda for the 1st Brigade of the ABiH. And you questioned him relating to media matters. Who had arrested him? Why was he arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know at that moment why he had been detained and for what reason. Quite simply, he was at Heliodrom, and I interviewed him at Heliodrom. However, I cannot give an answer as to why he was at Heliodrom and who detained him. We only received information from the SIS that he could be of interest to us from the point of view of the Crime Department. However, we did not find any relevant elements, and that is why the record looks as it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vidovic, I'm somewhat surprised by your answer, because you conducted a very comprehensive interview, over two pages, approximately. There's a lot of information in here. The interview must have lasted quite a while, and you didn't even ask yourself why this person was a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply don't know why he was detained. I did not detain him. And from the point of view of our department, he was not of interest to us at all. None of us would have detained him, and I did not have any information that would lead me to detain him, or anyone from my department. So he was not of interest at all from the point of view of the Crime Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have 12 minutes left, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to document P03038 [as interpreted]. That is six documents ahead. Have you found it? It is a report that you are sending to the Military Police Administration on the 6th of July. We see that it was received on the 8th of July, 1993. And this report says -- P03238 is the document that I'm looking for. And in the one-but-last sentence, around the middle of the paragraph, it says: "I have to add one more thing; namely, that during the course of the day yesterday, on the premises of the SVIZ, a written report was received, signed by Colonel Obradovic, pointing out that without his signature, no visits or releasing of detainees from the SVIZ Heliodrom could be carried out. I seek further instructions from the Military Police Administration regarding this order." Do you recall this, and what can you tell us in this regard?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a special report, because in our regular work, the regular work we carried out on the premises of the Heliodrom, we had certain duties every day; that is to say, to deal with detained soldiers from the scope of our authority and to file criminal reports if there were grounds for that. Here, we have a new situation. People from the administration of the Heliodrom are suggesting to us that we turn to our own administration, because as of the following day already, we would not be allowed to enter the premises of the Heliodrom. From the very next day, we would not be allowed to enter the Heliodrom. We would have to ask Colonel Obradovic for special permission. By then, he was near Stolac, and that is over 40 kilometres away from Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you do something at that point of time? But please give me shorter answers because I have very little time left.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through our battalion, we addressed the operations zone directly and we explained the complexity of our situation, and we asked for Colonel Obradovic -- or, rather, the operative zone to allow us to enter the premises and conduct interviews; that is to say, we, the employees of the Crime Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you receive such permission and did you carry out your work as previously?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soon after that, we were allowed to enter, along with a special permission that he sent the administration of the Heliodrom, that the Crime Department employees could enter the Heliodrom and carry out their duties every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like us to move to P05054.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to draw the attention to a mistake probably in the translation. On line 10 of the previous page, it was translated that there arrived a written "report" of Mr. Obradovic, but I think it was an order rather than a report, "zapovjed."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is correct, it had to do with an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P05054 is the document we're looking at now. It is a report dated the 14th of September, 1993. We see that it's sent to you. We see that under number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And it says here: "On the 11th of September, we received information from the so-called private prison in Bijelo Polje." Please tell me whether you recall this, and do you know anything about this private prison, Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards this document, I just have to add that the prison warden was writing to me non-stop. It is very important to know that he was writing to me throughout his work, although this did not directly pertain to me, but he was writing to me non-stop. So he wrote to me about this prison in Bijelo Polje, and I, through the command of the town defence, I tried to find out what was going on, because Bijelo Polje was on the front-line. It is physically impossible to go there except in an armoured vehicle that was used to transport military troops to the front-line, so all the way up to the very last point that could be reached, and then this armoured vehicle would be taken. I'm sending this document to Mr. Mijo Jelic, who is replying to me that this is not his zone. After that, I tried to go to Bijelo Polje, but I was returned from the check-point, because I wished to know, in view of the fact that I first heard about this in my work, this was the first time that I heard of the existence of a private prison. After I was returned by soldiers from this last check-point before entering this armoured vehicle, I addressed the operative zone in writing, and very soon I got a response from them, stating that that was within the scope of their authority and that they would check what this was all about. Also, I sent them this document from Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like us to move four documents ahead to document 5D042 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document we've seen with another witness already -- [B/C/S spoken on English channel] -- actually a private prison. You have just explained to us that you tried to discover more about -- [B/C/S spoken on English channel]. Let me repeat. Witness, we have already seen this document with another witness. At the time, I was surprised to see that there was a private prison. You have just told us, by giving us a lot of detail, what you actually did to try and elicit this question. What I would like to know is this: Did you send a report to Valentin Coric to let him know what was going on? Did you actually do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said a moment ago, since this was a new situation as far as I was concerned, I tried to investigate. And based on my sources for a day or two, I even wanted to go to the location, and I told you how one could get there. It was the front-line, so if you use an APC, this is an indicator of the danger that it posed. So I did what I could within my remit. Let me repeat, I informed the commander of the defence of the town, first of all. When he said it wasn't in his area, then I informed, through the battalion, the operative zone, and all the reports from the battalion were sent officially, with the official post, to the operative zone. I did not inform the Military Police Administration at that time because I considered that I could get all the necessary information and instructions from the operative zone because we were dealing with the front-line and combat directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It took you approximately three minutes to tell me that you did not send a report to Mr. Coric. You could have told me this in a split second. This is what I wanted to know. Can one, therefore, conclude that Mr. Coric was then not aware of the existence of this private prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's move ahead now several documents until we reach 5D04233, the third document from the end of the binder. Have you ever heard of somebody called Reuf Ajanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of Reuf Ajanovic, A-j-a-n-o-v-i-c. It's somebody who was in the Convicts Battalion, and he introduced himself as some sort of internal security officer of the Convicts Battalion, a sort of SIS person from the notorious battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: When you went to Heliodrom, did you see that person there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went to Heliodrom, the practice was that through the prison warden, we would announce our arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, did you see him or not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw him at Heliodrom, on the premises of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Reuf and Mr. Praljak knew each other?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Josip Praljak several times with Mr. Reuf Ajanovic sitting together in an office.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Was there an investigation underway including Mr. Ajanovic and Mr. Praljak together?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in the autumn of 1993, some documents went missing from the Military Investigative Prison of Heliodrom, Remand Prison of Heliodrom, and I think that an investigation was underway investigating the two men about these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I have two more questions for you. We're going to look at just one document, to P03613. Did you know that the place Otok Vitina, that there was a prison there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just heard of it, but I was never there physically.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Kresimir Tolj?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He worked in the Crime Department of Ljubuski and later on headed the Crime Investigation Department of the Ljubuski section, like I was in Mostar, so my colleague and opposite number.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Did you see him frequently, Mr. Tolj, and co-operate with him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We co-operated fairly frequently in our line of business, especially after July. So throughout October -- throughout August and September we frequently co-operated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as head of the department yourself, did you have the authority to appoint the warden of a prison? And if so, did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not within our remit. We never appointed any warden of any prison, nor did we have the authority to appoint prison wardens.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now look at document -- the one in front of you, which is signed by Mr. Kresimir Tolj. And it says: "Re. Appointment of the head of the Military Prison Otok." And from the document, it follows that Mr. Tolj is, in fact, appointing a man by the name of Kreso Medic. May I have your comments on that, because you've just told us he didn't have the authority to do that? Have you heard about this?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, I've never heard about this. And it's an impossible situation, as far as I'm concerned. I see that it says "Military Police Administration, Crime Prevention Department," and it doesn't say "Ljubuski," whereas Kresimir Tolj worked in Ljubuski. And then there's a handwritten number and the letters "FK." We didn't have any letters like that, no "FK." So I'm bewildered by this document. It's not clear to me at all. And I'm sure that Mr. Kresimir Tolj couldn't do anything like this, occupying the post that he occupied.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you know the man Kreso Medic mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know who the person is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, sir. That completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have just another question for you. We can see that you have addressed a number of reports to the military prosecutor. We also know that when some crimes are committed, the investigating judge came to the scene. What I wanted to know is whether you had any contact with the military prosecutor, the investigating judge, and the military judges. Were these people with whom you had talks about the investigations or were these people you never saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you the following answer to that question: In our service, we had all the telephone numbers and addresses of the persons that you mentioned, who we contacted if we needed to call them for anything, an eye-witness account or whatever. We just contacted them in writing, but we did have a few meetings, that is to say, our department, the MUP, and the representatives of the military prosecutor and military investigating offices, working to uncover as many crimes as possible and deal with as many criminal reports filed as possible. So some people from the courts and the Prosecutor's Office I did meet at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, as far as other Defence teams are concerned, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. I do have some questions for the gentleman. If I may begin, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Michael Karnavas and with me is Ms. Suzana Tomanovic, and together we represent Dr. Jadranko Prlic. I just have a few questions, and if you could be rather brief, I would most appreciate it. There are only, I believe, four documents we will look at. But before we get to the documents, as I understand from listening to your testimony, there was co-operation between the military police with the civilian police concerning investigations of crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can I take it, then, from your answer that to some extent the civilian courts were functioning at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were functioning, just like the civilian police was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before I get to the documents, I want to ask you a couple of preliminary questions. When a soldier left the front-line, was he still a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When he left the front-line, and on his way home, for instance, committed a crime, would he be considered a civilian or a soldier at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, he was at all times a soldier, so he would be considered, in your case, a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it, in that case, it would be the military police who would be responsible, at least to some extent, to do the investigation.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always his commander who was responsible for a soldier, and the military police would be involved if a crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it a commander, a commander, never informed you that you were not to investigate his soldiers once they left the front-line because they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already repeated this. The commander -- if his soldier committed a crime, it was the commander's duty, if he knew who the perpetrator was, to report him, to file a criminal report against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But my question is a little more precise than that, and what I want to know is whether you were ever instructed by anyone, any commander, low, medium, or way up high at the Main Staff, that once a soldier leaves a front-line, he's no longer a soldier, he's a civilian, and therefore you need not treat him as a soldier, you need not investigate the case.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not receive instructions like that, because we considered him to be a soldier, always a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just one last question on that. I assume that commanders were aware of that. In other words, this is not such specialised knowledge that only military police officers would be aware of that; the commanders would be aware of that as well?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. What for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you indicated that they continued to be soldiers. I assume that the commanders knew that.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the first document, and they may not be order, but there are only four. It's 5D04362, 5D04362. I believe it's the last document in your folder, the very last one. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Usher, if we could -- there is no -- usually, there should be a B/C/S version right after the English, but if you don't have it, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we can see that this is a document dated 26 May 1993. We see that it's been sent to the Defence Department and as well to the Operative Zone South-East Herzegovina. Now, I want you to first -- and we see that this is a report. Now, picking up where we left off, if we could go towards the bottom of the page at least in English, where it says: "At 2000 hours ..." We see that: "... a soldier without identity card was brought to the Police Administration by members of the Police Administration security, who was in a drunken state, armed with Argentina gun. He said he was from the 1st Battalion, Capljina. I called military police and handed him to them, together with the Argentinean gun number ..." And so on. Do you see that part, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, would this be a normal procedure? If a civilian police officer were to detain a soldier, would they then turn him over to the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this came within the remit of this police station, police administration, that among other things they should hand over the soldier to the military police. And this is a soldier from Capljina found in Mostar, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure that this was the correct procedure. Is that a yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next -- if we go all the way up to the text, where it says: "At 1800 hours," we see that Puce Nikola came to the Police Administration, an employee of the civilian prison, and reported that there were two detainees in investigation with him, but they were transferred to the Heliodrom due to combat activities, from where somebody let them go, and that would have been Josip Praljak. Now -- and my question is: Why would this occur? Why would they take civilian prisoners to the Heliodrom, keeping in mind that this is 26 May 1993? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says some Puce Nikola, working in a civilian prison. I think it's the civilian [Realtime transcript read in error "military"] prison that we, in Mostar, call Celovina. And at this point in time, the 26th of May, he was up at the front-line. So that's Santic Street, where heavy fighting was going on, and I think that prison was relocated because of the war to Heliodrom, the entire prison was moved, because it was impossible for it to function because it was right up at the front-line. The prison wall was up at the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I have to correct the translation, which I believe it is important to do at this stage. On page 25, line 10, the witness said that Puce Nikola was working in a civilian prison, and in the transcript it was erroneously recorded as "military prison," which is an important difference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just real quickly before we leave this document, yesterday you were asked several questions about identifying, perhaps, the ethnicity of individuals. If we look at this report and we see that there are 17 names that were injured, and can you identify whether, on this list of 17, there are any of Muslim Bosniak nationality; according to the name, that is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can see that. Number 1, a Bosniak Muslim; number 6, Fedad Salkovic, Bosniak Muslim; number 16, Fuad Kadija, a Bosniak Muslim; and number 17, Fatima Mujcic, a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we go to the next document, and this document is 5D04152. 5D04152. And my apologies for not having them in order. I just reorganised my cross this morning. Do you have it, sir? And you should have the B/C/S version perhaps after the English. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I spoke to you earlier about whether the courts were functioning, and you indicated that you thought that they did. Now, I want you to look at this document. We see that this is an indictment, and if we look at -- if you look at it very quickly, and you'll see a number 2, for instance, the victim seems to be an Esad Hadziosmanovic, and I assume he's a Bosniak Muslim from the name. Now, from looking at this document, can you tell us whether, to the best of your knowledge, this is what an indictment would have looked like at that time, given the situation as it existed in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the indictment from the Senior Public Prosecutor's Office, I can't tell you what that should look like. All I can say is at the beginning of 1994 I left the unit I was working in until then, went to Zagreb for military training, and I assume that this is the kind of indictment that the Senior Public Prosecutor's Office in Mostar would issue. I assume that it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the name Esad Hadziosmanovic, and it talks about in Mostar, and you are from Mostar, do you know this gentleman ?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about the street, where it looks like -- where it says that -- where his residence is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The street is in West Mostar, Brace Bosnjic Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the next document, which is 5D04241, 5D04241, this is dated 20 October 1993, and we see that at the top "Senior Public Prosecutor's Office, Mostar." If you go to the last page, we see that there is a station commander, Mladen Alpeza. Do you know this gentleman, by any chance, or are you familiar with the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him personally, because at the time we co-operated with the Police Station of Mostar quite often. Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in looking at this document, granted as to when you left and what your function was with the military police, would this confirm, at least in your mind, what you were saying earlier, that the civilian police was investigating as the military police was?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the last document I want to look at 1D03155, but before we look at the document, itself, I need to ask you one or two questions. Now, keeping in mind that you left, I believe, in late 1993 from the military police, did there ever come a time, in 1996 and thereafter, where it became known in Bosnia-Herzegovina that arrests of suspected war criminals could not take place without prior authorisation from this particular Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the beginning of your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did there come a time in 1996 when it became known that suspected war criminals, or those who were suspected of committing crimes during the war, could not be arrested and indicted without the international community giving its authorisation?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Did you ever hear about the rules of the road --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I understand the question that was just asked regards procedural matters after 1996, a period of time where this witness was no longer in the HVO and certainly was not involved with international matters or prosecution. I understand that Mr. Karnavas is probably about to ask questions about 1903155. This witness had no authority to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the Rome Agreement and the rules of the road?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the Rome Agreement, but just as a citizen. That's all I can tell you. I don't know anything more about the agreement, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when you say "as a citizen," you don't know any of the particulars; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I've heard of the name, "Rome Agreement," but that's all. I don't know any details of the agreement or anything like that. I didn't know about it then, and I don't know about it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it if I were to ask you whether you heard about the rules of the road, you would give me the same answer.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. 2D.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all in the courtroom. May I just have a moment, please. Could the usher please take this material so that we could organise our examination. Once again, I would like to greet all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, these are the documents that we will be using. Before I start putting questions to you, I would just like to make a correction in the transcript. My learned friend Mr. Karnavas said, on page 24, in line 2, in relation to document 5D4362, obviously mistakenly said that this report was sent to the Defence Department. However, we see from the document that it was actually sent to the Operations Zone of South-East Herzegovina. We can see that on the basis of the receipt stamp. That's the only correction I had. Witness, could you please look at the first document in my binder, and that is P665. There aren't very many documents, and it's going to be easy for us to find our way. This is an order of Mr. Bruno Stojic, dated the 26th of October, 1992, which says: "Pursuant to the agreement reached with the representatives of the International Red Cross, the EU, and UNPROFOR monitors ..." He ordered that: "All prisoners of war held by the HVO be unconditionally released from HVO military investigation prisons." He said that this would take place on the 30th of October, 1992, in the presence and through the mediation of the representatives of the International Red Cross and EU and UNPROFOR monitors, from the HVO prisons in Mostar, Livno, and Tomislavgrad. In relation to this topic, I'm going to show you another document, and then I'll put a question. The next document is P677. This is a report that Mr. Valentin Coric sent to Mr. Bruno Stojic on the 31st of October, 1992. It has to do with the release of prisoners on the 30th of October, and it says -- or, rather, there's a reference to Mr. Stojic's order. And could we just look at the last paragraph of the document, which is a sublimation of everything that matters. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We can no longer hear counsel. There are other microphones on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Livno, Mostar and Tomislavgrad. In the presence of the representatives of the International Red Cross and the EU and UNPROFOR monitors, it says that a total of 363 prisoners were released. Out of them, 285 prisoners have been sent to the so-called Yugoslavia, and 78 have been released and are still "on our territory." That is what is stated in the document. Mr. Vidovic, do you have any knowledge to that effect, and do you know that on the 30th of October, 1992, prisoners of war were unconditionally released?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say the following: This is when I started working at the Crime Department of the Military Police. I know about these unconditional releases, that they did take place: As a matter of fact, I was at the Heliodrom on one day and I saw, with my very own eyes, how these buses were leaving. I did not take part in this directly, but I do know that this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, tell me, who were these prisoners of war? According to your information, who were they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were imprisoned members of the Serb Army, the Yugoslav People's Army, who were taken prisoner in the summer of 1992 by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It was the TO that was fighting with the HVO in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I assume that these were joint prisoners.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you to look at document 1D -- let me just see whether you can confirm something for me. 1D2435. Have you found it? This is an agreement on the release and transfer of prisoners from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it has to do with these persons that we referred to just now. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is sending this to Minister Susak on the 2nd of October, 1992, but let us look at the first page of this document. As far as I know, you can follow, in English, what it is that I'm asking you about. It is obvious that the agreement was reached. We see that on page 1. And there is a reference to the persons who were present on that occasion. The third name is Mr. Sito Coric, representing Mr. Boban. We are going to skip the actual agreement, and please let us go to Annex 1. That is roughly page 6.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm repeating the name of the document, 1D2435.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine says "10."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's all right. Have you come to the page where Annex 1 is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Activities after --"

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sorry that the pages haven't been numbered. There is a number at the bottom of the page. It should be 1D51-0487.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found it? It says "List of places of detention, according to information given by detaining parties. Since we saw from the previous report there was a reference to Mostar, Livno, and Tomislavgrad, and we see that here under number 2; right? We see those places? Very well. Could you please just give us a verbal answer, because just nodding cannot be recorded in the transcript. In footnote 1, it says that all detainees from Capljina, Tomislavgrad and Livno would be transferred to the Mostar Prison --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, I would like to say -- I would like to correct them. It says that they had been transferred. It's the perfect tense.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You saw that in Mostar, that they were leaving the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the buses that were leaving the Heliodrom, the buses with these prisoners of war who were about to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us just confirm something else. Could we please have a look at Annex B. It is two pages later. 1D51 is the page, 0490. There is a reference here to places of detention and possible routing. There is a reference to Mostar down here. On the next page, we see a reference to Tomislavgrad and Livno. Finally, my question, Mr. Vidovic: Can you confirm that just as we saw in this agreement, that this agreement, indeed, was a basis for the release of the prisoners whom you saw and who were released on Mr. Stojic's orders?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now please look at another document, P619. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a daily report of Mr. Valentin Coric for the 22nd of October, 1992. I would be interested in paragraph 2. I'm going to ask you about paragraph 2. It says: "According to the order of the head of the Defence Department, on the basis of a decision made of the Presidency of the HVO, we captured the following features in town during the day: The Post Office building, the building of the MUP ..." And so on. And the end of the penultimate paragraph says: "In the entire action, no one was wounded or killed. Some people were brought in by force, without fire being opened." Mr. Vidovic, I remember that you started working at the Crime Department sometime in the beginning of October. Tell me, have you heard of this operation?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of this operation. It was a security operation that was basically aimed at the following. We see a reference here to the Post Office building, so these are the vital organs of the town of Mostar. If we look at the date, the 22nd of October, 1992, that would roughly be the time after direct fighting against the Serb forces had stopped and life was slowly returning to the town of Mostar. Some telephones had just started working. We have had a bit of electricity by then in apartments. So I think that this was a security operation that was just meant to stop certain groups from messing with the Post Office and other important buildings, if I can put it that way. There is a reference here to the fact that there were no persons wounded, no fatalities, that fire was not opened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, my understanding was that this had to do with a police action in order to secure some vital facilities.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please explain to Their Honours what the Post Office looked like - and that was certainly a vital facility - at the moment when the conflict was over between the HVO and the BH Army, on the one side, and the Serb forces, on the other side? What did the Post Office look like?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Post Office and all the vital buildings and facilities in Mostar had already been shelled in April, May, and June 1992. The Post Office had been shelled, and it had to be renovated; not only the Post Office. Department stores were set on fire due to the indiscriminate shelling in 1992. Also, churches were set on fire by the indiscriminate shelling that took place. People were killed all the time by indiscriminate shelling. I have to add here that my own father was killed in July 1992 and that he was a casualty of indiscriminate shelling. So I repeat, the Post Office, like all other key buildings and institutions in the town of Mostar, was almost destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, from the point of view of security, was there a large number of people in town? After these first clashes, was there an increase in crime, and did thieves, criminals, unauthorised persons, break into these buildings? I mean, I know you were wounded at the time, you were a citizen. So to the best of your knowledge, what happened? What was the situation like after the conflict with the Serbs in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you followed what I said yesterday carefully, you would have heard that there were these big trade centres for technical equipment that refugees ultimately moved into. The town was full of refugees. When these people arrived, the security situation became far more complex than it would have been otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Witness, my apologies. It took me a while to put this question to you, but you just said that your father was killed in July 1992. Your father was living in which part of Mostar at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, you asked me, and I told you that we lived in the western part of town, in the part of town that is called "Rondo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as you know, did the Serbs carry on shelling the city of Mostar, and especially Western Mostar, but also East Mostar, during the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb forces shelled Mostar throughout the war, without any difference between the eastern and western side. So throughout the war, after the month of June, when they withdrew with their forces from the eastern part of town. That is to say that we had this border on the Neretva. After they withdrew from the plateau above Mostar, from Podvelezje, they shelled the town of Mostar all the time, indiscriminately, without taking time into account or the number of shells that had fallen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, between January 1993 and December 1993, was there, in West Mostar, victims, Croats, that is, that fell under Serb shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Yesterday, you said that there were several thousands of Muslims in West Mostar. As far as you know, amongst this Muslim population in West Mostar were there any victims of Serb shelling between January 1993 and December 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot give an answer to that, whether this was amongst the Muslim population only. But I know that among all of the citizens of Mostar, including the western part, there were victims of the Serb artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I see the time, but I just have two or three short questions in relation to this document and then we can take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, we are going back to this now. The Honourable Judge asked you about 1993, but we're going back to October 1992. Tell me, in that period in Mostar, were there any clashes with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, and later on for as much as you know.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, after the HVO, together with the Mostar Battalion, took part in the operation to liberate Mostar in mid-June 1992, we held the line facing the Serbs, the Serb enemy, and Serb Army, together on the Podvelezje Plateau. And until the conflict broke out on the 9th of May, we held the line together facing the Serb Army; the whole length of the Mostar battle-front, which stretched from the northern entrance to town to the southern exit from town, the hills around Mostar in the eastern part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, although you didn't expressly say that in response to my question, but we can conclude that there were no clashes between the HVO and the BH Army from that period right up to May, as you said?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, there were no conflicts until the 9th of May, 1993, between the members of the Mostar Battalion and the HVO forces in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, just one more question on that subject. Do you know whether the HVO took part with the BH Army in this period, roughly, that is to say, around October 1992, in any larger military operation against the army -- or, rather, the Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of one particular operation. I don't know what it was called, but there was a military operation which was launched sometime at the beginning of November 1992, I believe, in the area above Blagaj. And Blagaj is a place which is 12 kilometres away from Mostar, roughly south-east of Mostar, and the object of that operation was to move the front-lines of the Serb Army towards Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, was that operation led together with the BH Army and the HVO; did they work together, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mostar Battalion and the HVO of Mostar took part together in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I tell you that it was Operation Bura, does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, and I think it was November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [In English] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, please take a look at the following document in the binder, 5D2013. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, yesterday, during your evidence on page 8, lines 14 through 16, you spoke about Zeljko Dzidic and the information that you had, that he was suspended at some time in April 1993. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was suspended because of a row he had with some soldiers from Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have this document before us. It's entitled "Conclusion." HVO of the municipality of Siroki Brijeg, at its meeting dated 23 April 1993, discussed the letter received from the Command of the Siroki Brijeg Battalion, and, with relation to that, adopted the conclusion that the HVO of Siroki Brijeg condemns the brutal and cruel act of the military police toward the soldiers of the Siroki Brijeg Battalion, which happened on the 15th of April. In item 2, they request the competent bodies to suspend Commander Zeljko Dzidic of the military police, and the launching of an official investigation in order to clarify this incident, and they request that the competent authorities act urgently and report on what has been done. Mr. Vidovic, is that the incident that you mentioned which happened between Zeljko Dzidic and the Siroki Brijeg Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is this very incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll take you back to your job now within the Crime Prevention Department in Mostar. And please take a look at document 5D5022. That's the following document. This is a criminal report drafted by your department, dated the 21st of August, 1993, against Jeton Berisa. He was also a member of the Convicts Battalion Krusko, and he is in detention, which follows from the information below his name. The second person's name is Drazenko Farc. There is a description of the offence. These two persons allegedly went to the apartment of one Ziga - that's his nickname - of Muslim ethnicity in order to steal some objects from that apartment. The incident happened in the night of 12 to 13 August 1993. You qualified this offence as violating a private home, the privacy of the home. Can you remember this incident, and did your section work on this case?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document of our section. This incident happened, and we processed it in our section.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please take a look at the following document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm a bit surprised that this should be the incident which prompted the letter of Siroki Brijeg, because in that letter they speak of cruel behaviour, and breaking into a house is certainly against the law and all, but it is not exactly a brutal and cruel act. So, Witness, can you explain this discrepancy or can you tell me what I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're referring to a different document. This document of Siroki Brijeg is totally unrelated to the document in which breaking and entering is mentioned. My learned friend has passed on to another topic, and this other document, which is four months older, has nothing to do with it. These are two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this intervention, Ms. Tomasegovic. I was at a loss because I never saw the words "cruel act" in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at document P6873. Mr. Vidovic, today and yesterday you spoke extensively about the District Military Prosecutor's Office, the contacts you had with them, and co-operation, and how your section filed criminal reports with them. This is a letter of the district military prosecutor, dated the 25th of November, 1993. It was sent to the Ministry of Justice and Public Administration, and it says: "Following your request," number so-and-so, "we submit the following information: "In the period from the 16th of June, 1993, through 24 November 1993, the Office of the Prosecutor received 539 reports against members of the MOS as follows:" And then some names are mentioned. I don't believe that it is necessary to mention anybody's name in open session. But take a look at this document, since this is a very relevant period from 16 June until 24 November 1993. Most of this time, you were in the Crime Prevention Section. Can you remember, based on this document, that these were criminal reports filed by your section?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first two pages of this document, I recognise numerous persons against who we filed criminal requests. That's only about pages 1 and 2. And if I were to review the rest, I believe I would find a significant number of people on whom we had criminal files. As far as I can tell, this is in alphabetical order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, it's in alphabetical order, but the alphabet was not fully complied with. But I'm satisfied with your answer anyway. Let's move on. Mr. Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: One short question, Witness. Looking at these names in a superficial way, I get the impression that most of them are Muslim names. Am I wrong again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have looked at the list of these 539 -- I believe it's 539 names. Seemingly, the prosecutor withdrew one, Goran Jelavic, number 56. You, as a legal expert, I would like to know whether, in your view, these 539 people fell under the authority of the prosecutor regarding any potential detention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know under whose authority they were with regard to detention. But as you're asking me about the remit of the Public Prosecutor's Office, if they were at Heliodrom as perpetrators of crimes, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that if these 539 people were suspected of a criminal offence, in that case they fall under the authority of the prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, in that case, would there not have to be an order of arrest, an arrest warrant, which should ultimately, I think, emanate from a judicial authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat? I haven't fully understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was a bit fast. You say they were detained -- yes, detained under the authority of the public prosecutor. My question is: Did the public prosecutor alone have the authority to send people to detention or should there not be an arrest warrant which is issued by a judicial authority; the Military District Court, probably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is about the District Military Prosecutor's Office, so we can assume that these were -- these were military persons, military staff, and criminal reports were filed against them for criminal offences. That's the only thing I can tell, and I wouldn't want to speculate about any other aspects. This is only about criminal reports filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly. And to me, there must be a link between a criminal report filed and a title for detention. Normally, in criminal procedure, the fact that you file a criminal report against a suspect is not enough to put him in prison, but maybe it was different under the law applied here. But that I would like to know. Maybe you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but if we take a look at the lists, if we skim through them, at the moment when this letter was being compiled -- or, rather, the fact that it was compiled doesn't prove that these people were all put in detention, because there are names of people here who were not detained. So this is not a list of people who were detained. It's a list of people against whom criminal reports were filed for various offences, criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, let us clarify a bit. The first question of Judge Trechsel was whether this is mostly about Muslims. Let us return to page 1. And on page 1, we can read that these are members of the MOS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, so there's no doubt about that. And then a criminal report can be filed against a person who you cannot arrest because that person -- you can't get to that person?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I want to say. And for -- out of respect toward the deceased, the person under number 1 was a member of the ABiH, and a criminal report was filed against him in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Take a look at the names under 35 and 36 on page 2. We don't need to mention the names. Under 35, you see a person against whom a criminal report was filed, and that person is still not arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Under 36, there is a person against whom a criminal report was filed for war crimes, and do you know that he was arrested only recently for crimes committed in Trusina?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I learned from the media that this person was arrested for the crimes committed in Trusina and that he is, I believe, in the prison of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us be completely clear. This is a list of criminal reports, but not a list of detained persons?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Vidovic, in the examination-in-chief you spoke a lot about criminal reports against unknown perpetrators. You said that to you these cases were not closed until you found the perpetrators. Tell me, when a prosecutor received such a report, was he duty-bound to act based on that report against unknown perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon reception of a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator, or NN, the public prosecutor was duty-bound to do everything from the domain of that criminal report, send out letters, request information from the authorities in charge, and do everything to identify the perpetrator. I also said yesterday that we, too, in going about our work and working on other cases, found new information that would have to do with another case, that NN case, and it wasn't such a rare occasion. So these NN cases were not closed for us ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, could you tell the Bench that there was a large number of cases against NN perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a very large number of cases involving NN perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You explained to the Bench the conditions under which you worked in Mostar in 1993. Let us not repeat all the details. These conditions, many soldiers passing through, coming and going, had that -- did that have a direct impact on your inability to find the perpetrator of a criminal offence within a reasonable time-period?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
