utterances.text: Yes. Well, these wartime conditions and our poor technical equipment certainly affected that. But, on the other hand, we had a strong will to work and be efficient, and the result was what you have outlined.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I will now ask you, as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you know that at this moment, as we speak, there is a number of criminal offences in your town, Mostar, or in Sarajevo, terrorist attacks and the like, in which cases the perpetrators have not been found for years?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are completely right. It's just as you said. Even today, a large number of criminal offences still involves unknown perpetrators, not only in Mostar but all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. I can speak about that as a citizen only, because I haven't been with the police for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you as a citizen, because you also know that a number of international organisations provided assistance to the judiciary and the law enforcement agencies so that now they have modern equipment, and a register of citizens and their IDs, so that even today, under excellent conditions, it still happens that the perpetrators of some serious crimes remain undiscovered for years; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, let's now -- well, let's see what happened to cases which you sent to the military prosecutor and on the basis of which criminal procedure was initiated. I'm going to show you three documents now which are going to show that they continued to act in those cases even when the military courts and Military Prosecutor's Offices ceased to function. So look at 5D5032 now, please. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you see the document, the minutes, during the proofing session, this record? I'm asking you that because, if need be, we can take a little time to look through it. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: These are the records written by the Military Court in Mostar, dated the 31st of July, 1995, and it says it has to do with the transfer of cases, the archive and documents, between the Military Court in Mostar and the lower court in Siroki Brijeg. Now, before that, let's establish some significant aspects of this. Although it's clear from count 42 of the indictment, but can you confirm that the Washington Agreement was signed in March?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vidovic, can you also confirm that in the Washington Agreement, which regulated organs within Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the judiciary system was set up, from the Supreme Court of the Federation down to the line to the lower courts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, after the signing of the Washington Agreement, in the preamble of this document, the military prosecutor says that he is handing over these cases to the basic court or lower court in Siroki Brijeg because that's the period when the military courts ceased to operate. Now, with this transference to Siroki Brijeg, and as we have three such documents, we'll take a look at what is being handed over. Uncompleted cases, that is number 1. Then we have uncompleted K cases, criminal cases. Then on page 2, completed and archived cases. And then it says "archived K cases," now I'm in 1992, those which had the force of law. And we see, in 1993, that this did exist, but can you confirm that the high prosecutor in Mostar was transferring to the lower court in Siroki Brijeg only those cases according to which the Siroki Brijeg lower court was in charge of?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then we come to 1995, 1992, and page 3 says that cases completed but not archived K cases, criminal cases, which means these are ones where the court passed judgement but did not archive them because some procedure was still lacking, and finally we see that Ivan Krstic signed, but the Siroki Brijeg court representative did not sign. And then we have at the bottom that the document was made in three copies. I'm going to show you three such records, and then I'm going to ask you my question. Look at 5D5024 now, please. The date's the same, and the same signatory on behalf of the Military Court in Mostar, because -- but here the cases are turned over to the Military Court in Capljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now move on to the next document, please, which is probably more interesting, and that is 5D5027. These are the minutes about the transference of cases, the Military Court in Mostar to the basic court or lower court in Mostar. It is being transferred by Ivan Kristic. I think he's Kristic, but it says "Krstic" here, president of the Military Court in Mostar. And let's see what he handed over: Incomplete cases, ongoing. There are none in 1992. In 1993, they were K cases, criminal cases, and here we have a large number of them from 1993 and 1994. On page 2, under "2," we have unfinished investigation cases, KI cases, where investigations were launched. Under "3," we have KI and KV, and then we have completed cases that were archived as well, and then K cases from 1992. And look at that list there, mostly in 1993. We have a long list, and also in 1994. But I'm going to stay with 1993 because you testified here and said that a large number of criminal reports, on the basis of which indictments were raised, that judgements were made in 1993, that they were filed in 1993; is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then we come to 1994, and under "3" which is page 4, it says completed or finalised, but not archived K criminal records. And then look at page 5, 1993. We have almost one and a half pages of the criminal cases, ones which you mostly worked on and your department; is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, from these records, it follows that the cases that you worked on, and ones in which indictments were raised and judgements made, on the 31st of July, 1995, were being handed over to the Municipal Court in Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, and Capljina for further processing. Is that what one can conclude from these documents?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, do you know that at these courts, the ones that were established following the Washington Agreement, and later on the Dayton Accords, that prosecutors worked there, and judges, of all ethnicity, both Croats and Bosniaks and Serbs and others? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber if we could move into private session for a few moments, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. There's an error in the transcript. On page 52, line 5, the witness said "he's my neighbour," not "he's my name." It should be "he's a neighbour of mine." That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, we saw, from the documents that I showed you and the names that we have now recalled of persons either working in the court still or used to work in the court, so some are still working, others have left, that they were Muslims. Now, this means, Mr. Vidovic, that the cases that you transferred -- or, rather, the president of the court in your name transferred, that work was continued on them -- these people could still work on them after the Washington Agreements and Dayton Accords; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we're interested in two cantons in particular here, and can you confirm, on the basis of your general knowledge, that the situation was the same in Travnik, in the Cantonal Court of Travnik, Travnik proper, and all the municipal courts that belonged to the Travnik region? Did they also carry on working after Washington and Dayton, that is to say, the members of all three nations/ethnicities in the judiciary, and are they still working?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now my final question, Mr. Vidovic. You told us, when asked by Mr. Tomasegovic when she showed you a document, you told us that the person, according to that indictment, to the best of your recollections, is still in prison today and serving the sentence they were sentenced to?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean, Ivan Bakovic, Ruda? Yes, yes, the Tomislavgrad/Mokronoge crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me Mr. Vidovic. I would have to search for the name in my papers. I did make a note of it, but I didn't have it in front of me. Does that mean, Mr. Vidovic, that after the signing of the Washington and Dayton Agreements, the BH Federation and Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted and took over all the cases and judgements made by judges in the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vidovic. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I think this question is very important, but the answer wasn't recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, just to avoid any misunderstanding, I'll ask you the question again. I asked you whether the judgements passed by the HZ-HB, after the Washington and Dayton Agreements, were they recognised by Bosnia-Herzegovina and honoured by Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and your answer was, Yes? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise for that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vidovic, regarding the last document, 5D5027, which is a report from the prosecutor, sending all the files to the civilian authority, I have noted, by looking at the year 1993, which is the year that is of interest to me, regarding cases that have been filed and completed, as well as cases which have not been completed -- or, rather, cases that have been completed, but unfiled - the former is in paragraph 2 and the latter are in paragraph 3 - all those files have a K letter attached to them. And I added up all these files. In the completed files and filed cases, we have 362, and for the uncompleted cases, or, rather, unfiled, we have 246 [as interpreted]. When you add them up, you come to 1.208 K files. So I repeat. For the files of paragraph 2, there are exactly 362. And for the files in paragraph 3, in total we have 846. When we add them up, we have in total 1.208 files. So, Witness, does that mean that during 1993, the military courts have tried 1.208 cases regarding criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the beginning you said that this was a report from the military prosecutor. It is not from the Military Court and the minutes and record. Now, to answer your question, if this has been listed here as it says here, there's only one thing that can mean; that it was done as you have just said. I've never seen this document before. I'm looking at it for the first time now, and it's not really my area, so I can't tell you more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. Although I finished, I think it would be a good idea to put another question in relation to the witness's knowledge. I'm still within the limits of my time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, with regard to these cases, were indictments issued and judgements passed in many cases against several persons? We are talking here about actual cases, not persons who were ultimately convicted, not the number of persons who were convicted. Do you know that there were several accused within one case?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw that yesterday, and we see that today. This number does not mean that it has to do with one person only. It has to do with a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The numbers that were added up by His Honour Judge Antonetti only have to do with Mostar, isn't that right, because he showed you a document where the Military Court is referring cases to the Municipal Court in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 3D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask for the usher's assistance so we could have these documents distributed, please. I'm not sure whether I will actually get to all of these documents. I think I have about 20 minutes, and I have some questions before that, so we'll see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My name is Bozidar Kovacic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have actually 18 minutes, not 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I wanted to give a round figure. I'm not as precise as you are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Bozidar Kovacic, and together with my colleague, Ms. Nika Pinter, I represent General Praljak, so I would like to put a few questions to you. First of all, let me, in part, continue along the lines of the questions previously put by my colleagues. On the basis of everything we've heard, especially during the cross-examination, is it correct that apart from the military police of the HVO that you discussed extensively, and the civilian police in the area of HZ-HB that you also mentioned, there was a police organisation that was a state police organisation with the same task of uncovering perpetrators in that territory in 1992/1993? So my question is: Are you the only two police forces that were in charge of doing that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to ourselves, the SIS and the Military Intelligence Service, VOS, also worked on the uncovering of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. But these two services that you mentioned just now are also organisations that work within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or let me say the authorities from Sarajevo, did they establish any police force for carrying out police work, either for the military or civilian sector, after the JNA aggression against Bosnia started?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Sarajevo is concerned and the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the establishment of its authority there, I don't have any major knowledge in this regard. I worked as a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, please follow my question carefully. In the area where you worked and where you live - this is a very simple question - we've mentioned the civilian and military police, and then you mentioned the SIS, et cetera. Was there any other police organisation, if I can call it that, that Sarajevo, as the government, as the capital of the state, organised to prosecute criminals, or are you the only organisation dealing with that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to say by way of a conclusion. I worked in the HVO, and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that with regard to this question, the period of time should be defined, the period defined that it refers to, when the police functioned and which one. The time-period should be specified. One would be up until the 9th of May and, say, another period would be after the 9th of May. And then the witness will be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank Mr. Coric for his suggestion. I will get to that, but my first question was whether the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina had ensured any police whatsoever. That is quite clear, and the witness had just started answering that question. And then I'm going to ask whether the situation was the same throughout. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, could you please answer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the third time that I'm trying to answer. I worked in the military police, and the military police of the HVO, the Crime Department and the Ministry of the Interior were the only two services that, at that period of time, dealt with crime in the zone where I worked and lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And just one more question in relation to that so that everyone would be clear on it. Had you not been doing that work - when I say "you," I mean the military police, the civilian police, and these other organs of the HZ-HB that you referred to - would anyone else be there to carry out that work or would there be total chaos and lack of order?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that the latter would prevail, total chaos and lack of order, had it not been for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I'm not going to pursue the matter further, because I think it is correct. I'm not interested in my new details. If Mr. Coric would like that to be dealt with, they can do it in redirect. My next question: In addition to all the details that you refer to, in terms of criminal proceedings, the powers of the civilian police, military police, the Prosecutor's Office, the investigating judge, about your own line of responsibility within the HVO, so you spoke with the operative zone and you said that the military police works in battalions, and you told us what your links were with the administration, in addition to that I'm going to put a very simple question to you so that you can tell us something in that regard. It's a hypothetical question. A commander of an HVO brigade commits a crime. Say he kills a person in front of everyone. Who arrests him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is arrested by the brigade military police. That is within their authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that it's the brigade military police, or is it any organ of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every brigade had its own brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Tell me, now -- we are dealing with this hypothetical killing, and it has to be dealt with. An on-site investigation should be carried out, the forensics and so on. Who will do that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, it's the Crime Department of the Military Police that gets involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. And, finally, who is going to file a criminal report with the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crime Department of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Tell me -- for a considerable part of the day yesterday and today, you spoke about different documents and your work in this connection. I am actually looking at something you said yesterday. Well, never mind. Let us not go into all this detail. Let's keep it simple. You and your colleague from the crime police, you are walking along a road and you see that a crime was committed. Say somebody is setting a house on fire or someone just killed a person. So I'm talking about serious crimes. At that moment, do you act ex officio or do you need instructions or approval from someone so that you could act?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We act ex officio within our official duty because that is our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So all the investigations that you carried out and all the criminal reports that you filed, and you -- and we see that you managed to do quite a bit of work there, did you do all of that on the basis of some initiative or some request or some order from the commander of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, in order for our work to be carried out at all, we needed to have knowledge of a crime. We received information from citizens, commanders of units, and also, as we've seen, in co-operation with the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. So can I put it in simpler terms; namely: Information concerning the commission of a crime and information that helped you get to the perpetrator of any crime, you would try to get that from any source?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move on to another topic. Yesterday, you said something about contacts with the brigade police. It is on page 78, in line 10 of the transcript. And a few moments ago, you mentioned this example of the arrest of the commander, that it would be the brigade police that would carry out that work. I would now like to ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I'm going to object in advance so that I don't have to be on my feet all the time. Yesterday, in direct examination, I asked the witness whether he was familiar with the establishment of the military police and whether he was familiar with the chain of command in the military police. He explicitly answered that he knew what had to do with his department and how orders were sent within his department. If -- well, the witness said now, as far as the remainder of the establishment of the military police, he is not familiar with that and he doesn't know who issued orders to who. So now I would like to ask that if my colleague wants to deal with that matter, I see that he prepared documents for the brigade military police and other relevant documents, could he please tell me what basis he has for that, how he laid the foundation for that. This has nothing to do with it, and it cannot be aimed at impeaching the witness, because the witness, himself, said at the very outset that he knew nothing about this topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond now? I remember full well the answer that my colleague referred to, and I even wrote it down. It was page 11, line 18 yesterday. However, in spite of that answer, yesterday, on page 78, in line 10, the witness said, in response to my colleague's question, that that was a record concerning an on-site investigation that was carried out by the brigade military police from Gornji Vakuf, and he specifically referred to a particular event and what happened. Also, a few moments ago, as you heard, in relation to my hypothetical question as to who would arrest the commander of a brigade if he committed a crime, the witness said the brigade military police. That is why I wish to put a few questions, and then, if necessary, I'm going to put other matters to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, as you said yourself yesterday, you are not familiar with the details of the establishment of the military police. But in spite of that, the fact that you had contacts with the platoon of the military police in the brigade is also a fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you know, and now you can tell me whether you do know or whether you do not know. So do you know that the platoon of the military police that existed within every brigade, and that is referred to in documents, and also people, when they talked about it, they referred to it as the brigade military police, do you know of that platoon having specific tasks, defined tasks, as the platoon within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I wouldn't want to go into that, what the platoon of the military police within the brigade did. That was not my own task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, since you are a lawyer, since you worked in the military police, and since you had contacts with the brigade military police, I'm going to ask you to look at this first document that I gave you, P04922. In order to provide information to all, may I say that this is already an exhibit. Could you please have a look at the document. Unfortunately, in the date there is no mention to the year. It just says the 10th of September, but we don't know what year. I believe it is from 1993. But if it is from 1992, yet again we're dealing with the same document. I would like to draw your attention to the first sentence in this text, and then I'm going to ask you the following. The first sentence says: "The delimitation of the field of competence within the military police," I underline that word, "within the military police," "the brigade military police is authorised:" And then the following are enumerated: Number 1, to secure barracks and commands; 2, military transports for the brigade; 3, enter into the front-line in the brigade's zone of responsibility; and, 4, the taking into custody and detention of individuals for the brigade. If you were an officer in the brigade military police, and given your level of training and education, would you understand this definition of what your task actually involved?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no heading, there is no year, this document is lacking, so it looks to me like some kind of an instruction that the Military Police Administration from Ljubuski is providing to a brigade or to all brigades with a view to the better establishment and work of the military police. There is something I have to add to that; namely, that the Military Police Administration gave administrative instructions on several occasions that had to do with the work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's interesting, but I don't have the luxury of time to carry on with that. Now, you didn't see the title, but it says, "Extract from Instructions on the Work of ..." It does say that. So judging by the style, you gave us the right description. And as everybody can see, it was signed by the chief, Valentin Coric. But let's go back to what we were discussing earlier on. From the tasks -- or, rather, brigade military police platoon described here, there's nothing about the kind of job you did, crime investigation, criminal processing, and so on. So looking at this document, I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness has answered the question and said that he doesn't know. Now, what does counsel want? Does he want the witness to read something that we can all read and we all know about or are we turning this witness into an expert, whether military or legal, I don't know; but he's a fact witness, he said what he knows during the examination-in-chief. He said he doesn't know the rules, regulations, and so on, so asking, Do you have the experience that the brigade military police did such and such, did you meet such and such, he can answer that. But to have rules and regulations read out to him, which he knows nothing about, I object to that. There's no sense in that. We can all read it. And having studied law, he worked exclusively as a military policeman for even less than one year, as we can see from his CV, so not before that, nor after that, did he deal in any aspects of the law. He's in the field of catering, and he's being called here as a fact witness to tell us what he knew about the period when he was working as a crime investigation policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know whether this document is dated 1992 or 1993. I can see that on the list of addressees, there is a 3rd, 6th, 7th and 8th Battalion. This is mentioned. This has also been sent to the 5th Battalion. This has been handwritten. The 3rd, 5th -- every time, I need to look at the transcript. It's difficult. I said 3rd, 5th, 6th, 7th and 8th Battalion. So, Witness, this document was sent to the 5th Battalion. Were you aware of this document or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at this document for the first time today, and everything I said about it, I said a moment ago, and I would like to stay with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document itself, there's a small sentence which says that the military police is unique and that there is a connection with the battalions and the companies. What do you think of this? It doesn't go beyond your field of competence, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Crime Department, I was also within the Battalion of the Military Police, as a member of the Crime Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, as we have no date on the document, but bearing in mind what His Honour the Judge has just put to you, and that it was sent to the 3rd, 5th, 7th and 8th Battalion, can you tell us what year it is? What year are we dealing with?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was added in handwriting, the names of the battalion, but I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not asking you to speculate. All right, I'll ask you the question differently. This is an exhibit already, so we don't need to question the authenticity of it. But it says a 3rd, 5th, 7th and 8th Battalions here. In 1992, were there eight battalions? Just say, Yes, or, No.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that way, because we have the 3rd MP Battalion and 5th Battalion, whereas until the 1st of July, I was in the 3rd Battalion and after the 1st of July, I was the 5th Battalion; 1993, that is. The 1st of July, the 3rd MP Battalion became the 5th MP Battalion, so that this addition in handwriting is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, you either didn't understand my question or you don't want to understand it, but let me go on. The 7th and 8th Battalions -- in 1992, were there eight battalions? Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what about after 1992, when there was a reorganisation; were there eight battalions?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. We could have settled that a while ago. But let's have a look at one more document now, or, rather, let me go back to my question before my colleague interrupted me. I didn't receive an answer to my question, and the question was this: A MP platoon, as described here in what we read out, it doesn't say anything about work in disciplinary matters, uncovering crimes, and so on, so do you stand by what you said, that the platoon deals with these legal and disciplinary things, offences? So for the crime part, the platoon -- the criminal investigation would ask for your department to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me? I have an objection. We're all having trouble with our LiveNote in the courtroom today, and I can't look at the document, open the document. But can we go back to the first page? Can we have the first page on our screens, because in the first paragraph, and I think I know this document well, that instructions are given as to what the brigade police does, which means apprehension and arrest for the brigade, and I think that is clearly stated and answers the question of what counsel is asking the witness now. And that excerpt was quoted by my colleague in the transcript, that that, too, was the work of the brigade police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see no grounds for that intervention, because I read out very carefully all the authority. But I've just asked the witness a different question, and I think, Witness, you answered in the affirmative, that hypothetical question of ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have no time left. You need to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would have finished a long time ago had I not been interrupted that frequently, because I have to go back to the same question. And when you have 18 minutes, that's impossible. But if I may be allowed to complete this question of mine. I don't know whether the witness understood the question, whether I was given an answer, but my question is as follows:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking, in the hypothetical case, the brigade police, the case when the commander committed a crime, whether he would be arrested by them, so for the more qualified work they would contact you, I mean, the Crime Investigation Department in the battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is the only work in the crime work undertaken by the brigade police, just the arrest, apprehension and arrest; that's all they do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we can call it crime work. The brigade military police is duty-bound to secure the crime scene, secure the traces, apprehend and arrest the perpetrator, if they are known, and then inform the Crime Investigation Department, which then continues the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's what I wanted to know. Your Honours, that completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question for you. I'm beginning to see things more clearly, but I would like to see things even more clearly than that by asking you a basic question. Let me make an assumption. Let's assume that a soldier goes home and discovers that his wife is with a lover. He kills the lover and his wife. Who has authority over this, the civilian prosecutor or the military prosecutor? This is a crime of passion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just repeat the beginning of what you said. Is he a soldier, is the person a soldier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he is a soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the perpetrator of a crime is a soldier, it will be the military prosecutor that has the authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if this is a crime of passion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see things much more clearly now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours and everybody else in the courtroom, and to you, too, Mr. Vidovic. On behalf of the Petkovic Defence, I'm going to ask you a number of questions and ask you to give us some additional explanations. You've told us a great deal, but I think that we can still add something.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, in response to Mr. Coric's Defence counsel, you spoke about the so-called private prison in Bijelo Polje on page 16 of the transcript today, and you told us that you tried to go there, but you were stopped, and that after that you went back to the operative zone and were given an answer and told that this would come within the authority of the operative zone and that they would check to see what it was all about. Have I interpreted your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti then asked you whether you had informed Mr. Coric about that, and you said that you informed the operative zone through the MP Battalion. My question to you is this: Did you, in fact, inform your military police battalion about this prison or the operative zone, as was your first answer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: In the daily reports compiled by the Crime Prevention Department to which I belong, at the end of each day we summarise our report through a daily report and we take it down to the battalion. When I say "take it down," we were in the floor above and they were downstairs. So that report, with all the other documents of the MP Battalion, is then sent to the operative zone and the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I'm not asking you about daily reporting now. I want you to tell me specifically. This information about the private prison, did you inform your MP Battalion or the operative zone thereof; you, personally, directly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We informed -- I, personally, directly informed, by written report, both the battalion and the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, did you directly send that report of yours to the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that went through the daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the MP Battalion sent these daily reports to the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, tell us this: Did you ever see a daily report from the MP Battalion which had written on it that it must be forwarded to and delivered to the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw that because I didn't work in those battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, did you ever see a report from the MP Battalion which would have on it a reception stamp of the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, how do you know that the MP Battalion sent its reports to the operative zone at all? Is that something that somebody told you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the time I was an operative in the Crime Investigation Department, I would receive that every day through my superior, and I mentioned it being Mr. Marcinko yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that, Mr. Vidovic. What I'm asking you is this: Do you have direct knowledge or were you told by someone? I don't mind by who. I'm not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. For the hundredth time, are you overlapping. You are speaking before the previous speaker has been translated, so you must make a break. Otherwise, things get lost, and time gets lost also.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no other way of interrupting an ongoing answer which I wish to interrupt, because every sentence uttered is deducted from my time, whereas I would just need one or two words in answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you have direct knowledge or did somebody tell you that the MP Battalion sends reports to the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have direct information only when I take over the Crime Department in Mostar and go to attend daily briefings in the MP Battalion in the morning, where we are assigned our daily tasks, and, among others, from the operative zone too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, did you ever attend a briefing at the commander of the operative zone's place?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us what the duties of a commander of a military unit were if a soldier belonging to that unit commits a crime. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please, does the same responsibility hold for the commander of a military police unit? Does he have the same responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And does the commander of a unit of the civilian police have to act in the same way?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, do you remember -- in the Law on Criminal Procedure, which was the Yugoslav law and was valid for all the republics in Yugoslavia, do you remember that this law provided for the fact that all state organs must submit criminal reports for crimes that are prosecuted in the line of duty, and that they are to furnish evidence along with those reports, and that they are duty-bound to secure the traces of a crime and cases -- or, rather, objects used in the commission of the crime? Do you remember that provision of the Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And that's to be found in document 4D1105, Article 148. And I'm saying that for the record. Mr. Vidovic, in your CV you mentioned that sometime in the beginning of November 1993, you were appointed head of department for the crime police in the Military Police Administration; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A proposal was made to that effect, but I was never appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then I misunderstood your CV. But could you please look at my set of documents now. You should have that binder somewhere. 4D2063 is the first document, 4D2063. Mr. Vidovic, I wasn't shouting at you. I was just repeating the number for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I don't have the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you would have to have that binder because we had it distributed during the break. [In English] Yes, four for Judges, because we delivered to all of them. The witness has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was right to put the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, let's look at this document. I do apologise, Your Honours, but I thought that it had been distributed already. Mr. Vidovic, this is a proposal to appoint an officer in the Military Police Administration. The date is the 11th of November, 1993. And under paragraph 10, a proposal is made to appoint Zvonko Vidovic. Witness, is this the proposal that you meant?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please look at the next document now, 5D4144. Tell me, Witness, can you recognise this document? Do you know what this is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document through which I am, in a way, relieved of duty in Mostar. And at a meeting in Ljubusko, I was told that I may be proposed for a new duty, and I was working on a survey of the work of our department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So that is your document; right? In the introductory part of this document, you say -- again, I have to correct the number of the document. 5D4114, 4114. Yes, now it's fine. So in the introductory part, you say that the military crime police assumed its final form in July 1993, and that it was subdivided into specialised departments and centres, and that it operated throughout the territory of Central Bosnia. Tell us, Witness, was the crime police truly reorganised in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us please look at the next document, P4544, P4544.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Document 5D4114, which stems from you, what drew my attention is this: This is something which could be of interest.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters like to note that they do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that this regards the statistical data, that there were 2.367 criminal reports. This is something you have to compare with the previous question relating to 1.208 procedures. This seemingly has to do with armed rebellion, Article 124. Article 119, serves an enemy army. Article 114, attack on the constitutional order. Article 120, aiding the enemy. Are all these articles and all these procedures related to the Muslim soldiers of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this document, I cannot see that. In such documents, we did not refer to ethnic backgrounds. In criminal reports, there is no reference, and especially not in this kind of document. This is quite simply an analytical review of what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Irrespective of this, did the Serbs or the Croats take part in an armed rebellion, did they attack the constitutional order, did they collaborate with the enemy, or don't you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just say that our legal department worked on criminal reports and sent them to the Prosecutor's Office. It is the Military Prosecutor's Office that ultimately qualified the crimes involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm trying to understand what this figure means, these 2.367 criminal reports. I'm trying to figure this out, and you aren't able to answer my question, when this document comes from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this document was created in my service, and I signed it as the head of the department. A certain number of people worked together with me, so on the basis of this document, I cannot say anything else, I cannot say more than this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, let us please look at P4544. This is a decision on call numbers in the Military Police Administration. It was passed on the 26th of August, 1993, by the chief. Let us look at number 10. Is that the department that you worked in, Mr. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostar Centre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mostar Centre, yes. Tell me, it seems to me, on the basis of this document, that the Mostar Centre that you worked in was part of the Crime Military Police Department in the Military Police Administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we look at page 2, we will see the 5th Battalion of the Military Police. And here, within the 5th Battalion of the Military Police, there is no reference to your centre; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, tell us now, if you can -- you said at the very outset that you worked in the 3rd Battalion and later on in the 5th Battalion of the Military Police. Can you explain this document to us, then, in view of your claim that you were actually part of the military police of the battalion? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain that. As I've said already, up until the 1st of July, we were under the 3rd Battalion of the HVO Military Police, and after the 1st of July, the 5th Battalion of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll look at the document after the break, because it's half past 12.00, and it would be the last break of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, let us look at the next document, 5D4110, 5D4110. This is an order that is being issued on the 3rd of August, 1993, by the chief of the Military Police Administration in order to improve the work of the military crime police, and it says also that it should be organised down the line, and also in terms of specialised departments as the crime military police is organised. My question for you is as follows: Did you know that the reorganisation of the military police was as described in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received this through the Military Police Battalion, the battalion I belonged to, and that's when we first came across this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, from then on it was no longer called the Department for Combatting Crime, but the military crime police?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to skip a few documents, and after this tab that you have - that's right - the first document is a report on the work of the HVO HZ-HB for the first half of 1993. In this courtroom, Mr. Vidovic, we did not have many opportunities to discuss the work of the civilian police, and since you did co-operate with the civilian police, I would like to take advantage of your presence here to show Their Honours what it was that the civilian police actually did. So could you please look at page 33. In English, it is page 21. It is the part of the report -- P4699 is the number of the document, 4699. So it's part of the HZ-HB report that refers to internal affairs, and A says: "The Police Section," and it describes the situation regarding law and order. My question for you, Mr. Vidovic: To the best of your knowledge, was the civilian police in charge of keeping law and order in the area of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A few pages on, 37 in Croatian and 24 in English, there is a reference to the Crime Investigation Section in the Department of the Interior. I'm going to give some of the information provided here briefly. It says a total of 1.438 criminal offences were registered in that period, and 153 various events which did not have a criminal character. Mr. Vidovic, could you explain this to us: When it says in this kind of report that certain crimes were registered, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the bottom of the page; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Crime Investigation Section. Does that mean that what had happened was recorded, were criminal reports filed? What was done in this regard?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, if they mentioned them this way, that means that they recorded them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then further on it says: "Out of the total number of criminal offences, 1.194 were common criminal offences, 52 were economic crimes, and 192 were crimes of special state concern." Witness, could you please tell us whether you know whether war crimes and terrorism fall under crimes of special state concern?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now please look at page 40, the end of page 40. In English, it should be page 27, if I'm not mistaken. It says: "Criminal police working on the prevention of crimes of special state concern (war crimes and terrorism) have filed to the competent Military Prosecutor's Offices a total of 192 criminal charges." My question for you, Mr. Vidovic: This may lead us to conclude that the civilian police also filed criminal reports with the Military Prosecutor's Offices?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You meant the civilian police, rather, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do apologise. I meant the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. And now the next document, P9411, 9411. These are instructions in terms of how the military police is going to act, when the Law on Criminal Procedure is in force, if there is a state of war or an imminent threat of war in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. My question for you is whether you were aware of these instructions, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this way. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the text. Number 2 says that: "The military police is duty-bound to carry out work related to: "1. Protection of life and personal property of people and property; "2. Prevention and uncovering of criminal offences; "3. Locating and arresting perpetrators of criminal offences; "4. Conducting investigations on the request of the judge of the Military Court and compiling a criminal file." Tell me, is this what you actually did?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, P42 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, could you give a date for this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, unfortunately, I cannot give a date. We can only base ourselves on the fact that there is a reference to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, so it has to be the period up until August 1993, but there is no date on this document. We tried to establish the date, but we did not succeed in doing that. For that reason, this document had not been admitted into evidence so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Exactly, and it also has no signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's why I'm not going to tender it either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Document P4275, please. This is a record from a working meeting that was held on the 18th of August, 1993, in the premises of the HVO of the HZ-HB in Mostar. The meeting was attended not only by members of the HVO, but others. We see Mr. Covic and Ivica Lucic, and the situation is the situation -- or, rather, the state of law and order in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. My question, Mr. Vidovic: The HVO, or later on the government, did it meet in Mostar in the second half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see from this document, yes, it did. However, in view of the combat going on, meetings were held in other towns of Herceg-Bosna as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, looking at the list of those present at the meeting, was there somebody there representing the HVO Army?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Valentin Coric, Ivica Lucic, and "P. Zelenika." Perhaps that's the Petar Zelenika, the one-time commander of the HVO of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in the second part, it says that on the basis of all information from the Defence Department staff and the staff of the Interior, it was assessed that there was better co-operation and co-ordination between the work of the military and civilian police and that operative plans were compiled to stop the trend of the rising crime rate. While we've still got it on our screens, the answer on page 82, line 9, the witness -- the answer wasn't recorded. He said "P. Zelenika" was Petar Zelenika, who was one-time commander of the HVO in Mostar. That's what the witness said, and it wasn't recorded. Okay. Now, I'm going to read another conclusion from this document under item 4. It says in the sphere of jurisdiction, more stringent measures should be enforced against people committing grievous crimes, such as murder, assault, and so on. And my question for you is: To the best of your knowledge, the organs of power and authority in Herceg-Bosna, did they really do everything they could, given the time and period, to uncover the perpetrators of crimes and to bring them to justice, to punish them for their acts against the law?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you two documents, after which I'll be asking you questions, the first of which is P5477. It's a letter from you, Mr. Vidovic, to the head of the Defence Department, dated the 29th of September, 1993. And the following document is 2D974, 2D974, of that same day, which you're sending to the Main Staff of the HVO, to General Zarko Tole. To start off with, if we look at the headings of those documents and try to define where the Mostar Centre is which you headed, tell us, Mr. Vidovic, was your Mostar Centre in the crime investigation military Police in the Military Police Administration or in the 5th Battalion of the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were still in the 5th Battalion of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why it doesn't say that in the head of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that we were still there, we were physically in the building where the 5th Battalion of the Military Police was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you were in the building of the 5th Battalion, but in establishment terms, you were in the Military Police Administration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it says here, then that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Tell me now, please, if you look at your stamp there, and on the stamp we can see that it is the Military Police Administration, which means there's no dilemma, in organisational terms, you were an organisational unit within the crime military police within the Military Police Administration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to put you right there. All our stamps, which were 22 stamps, were stamps of the 5th Battalion. We used all the stamped documents through the Military Police Battalion, we used those stamps sending them outside our department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now, looking at the contents of these documents, in both of them, on page 2, you say: "I would like to ask you the following, and I'd like to quote from the document sent to Bruno Stojic, that at top level a united position be taken with regard to the HVO units not interfering in military or civilian police affairs or in the military or civilian judiciary." Now I'm going to skip a line, and the next line reads: "At the highest level, to explain to unit commanders and who will, in turn, explain to their junior or senior officers, that within its domain, the police takes orders only from its chiefs." I'll end there. Everybody can read the rest. But tell us, please, Mr. Vidovic, are those really your words sent to the head of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a text that I compiled, wrote, sent, and signed, and sent it off to several addressees, because at that point in time I had -- well, I was experiencing daily problems in my department's work, as can be seen from the rest of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at the next document, which is 5D4115. And let's look at page 3 of that document. It is the minutes from the meeting held on the 21st of July, 1993, in the premises of the military police of the HVO in Mostar, and the representatives of the Internal Affairs Department attended the meeting, as did the Police Administration and the Police Station of Mostar, as well as representatives of the judiciary and the military police Mostar. My first question is this: Yesterday, Mr. Vidovic, and this was recorded on page 69 of the transcript, mentioned a meeting at the Military Police Administration on the 21st of July. Is that the meeting that is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness did not say meeting at the Military Police Administration. This was in the premises of the HVO of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. That's right. I wasn't very precise. No ill intention intended.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is that the meeting that you mentioned yesterday that took place in July and dealt with crime in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was initiated by the Ministry of the Interior of Mostar. It was held on the premises of the MP of Mostar, but they were the hosts. And a similar meeting, where we were the hosts, took place five or six days later with the same goals in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I think that was the 26th of July. We'll come to that, but let's look at these minutes first. You -- well, let's see what Mr. Vladimir Primorac, the commander of the Light Assault Battalion of the Military Police, has to say. He said that they were encountering similar problems as those of the civilian police and that they were coming across some independent ATG groups which were not part of the HVO units, and that it is known for certain that they were committing criminal acts. Mr. Vidovic, your personal knowledge, did it indicate the existence of these ATG groups that were outside the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's see what Mr. Penava says. He says: "The perpetrators of crimes are members of ATG groups, and the civilian police feels a certain amount of fear to enter into direct conflict with such persons. I do not know what the problem is and what is restraining the work of the military and civilian police, what's holding them back." Now tell us, Mr. Vidovic, these ATG groups, were they well armed and were they ready to fight the police if the police wanted to arrest them or prevent them in carrying out the crimes they were bent on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were prepared to do that, as you've just said. And the police was afraid of groups like that, especially the civilian police. And in the Mostar area, these groups would clash amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As we don't have time to read through all these reports in detail, I'm going to interpret one of the observations made of the civilian and military police. These acts, in the majority of cases, were done for gain, for purposes of gain, and that that's why there was a problem between these groups, who would have control over what territory and reap the most benefit, that is to say, steal as much as possible; was that it, in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in the conclusions from this meeting, which is on page 5 of the Croatian and the last page of the English text, among those under item 7, it says that, among other things: "The Defence Department must take a stand towards responsibility of the areas. One unit can control the front-line, while the rear is controlled only by the military or civilian police." Tell us, please, Mr. Vidovic, would that, in a relatively well-organised situation, be the rule, that the army is there to fight the enemy up at the front-line and that everything in the rear should be controlled by the military and civilian police forces?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Mostar, this could not be applied, because Mostar had a very deep zone behind the front-line, since the front-line stretched through the center of town and quite literally between the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell us, Mr. Vidovic, why, then, at this meeting, which discussed crime in Mostar, why were conclusions of this kind made, the primary conclusions, because it's a conclusion which relates to Mostar? Could you explain how that came about?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, the urban area was the defence line. However, Mostar is not such a small town, and throughout the war in Mostar areas in the town existed in which a decision of this type could be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well, Mr. Vidovic. Now a few documents about Mostar, itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I excuse me. I have a small question about this document. In the English text - they are not numbered - I think it's the fourth page, there is reference to what you have stated, Mr. Vidovic. And you have said, I quote: "If we, who had been appointed, had finished with collecting inhabitants in the city, it cannot happen that one unit or group is collecting people in the city." Now, I would like you to explain to the Chamber what you refer to by "collecting inhabitants in the city."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not the transcript. It's minutes signed by Javorka Ribica [phoen], a person I don't know, and I've never seen this before. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, while listening to you I was looking at the intervention of the president of the Military Court. It's very interesting. It's a president of a military court who takes the floor. I'm not going to go into details, but he talks about crime activities, he talks about Tuta, and so on and so forth, and he talks about the need to make sure that criminals are prosecuted. And then after him, somebody else takes the floor; namely, the military prosecutor, Naden Zuricic [phoen], and then he takes stock of the situation in a similar way. But I see that he talks about accusations against members of Muslim armed forces, but at the same time he doesn't really go into details. And then he says that there is no indictment against criminals of the city of Mostar, and he wishes that some repression be exerted. So these are those two highly-prominent persons that are touching upon issues that have been touched upon during the whole day. And then you're also going to take the floor and you're going to talk about an American who is going to visit the Heliodrom. Do you recall the intervention of the public prosecutor and the president of the Military Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When we read the time that they take the floor, we have the feeling that they would like more measures to be taken against those criminals. What's your take on this? Was that really the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already said, within my remit, as far as the department was able to, the one I worked in, we acted that way, we did do that. Now, of course, from the aspects of the present situation, that was not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The president is Velimir Maric. He may be a judge, I don't know, but he says something that is rather important. He says that policemen must be the first link when detecting crime, and then there should be the Crime Department, and the third link should be the prosecutor. So these are the three authorities that should play a role. That's according to him. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as it says here, he's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to our records, I have 11 minutes left. I was wondering whether I could be given an additional 10 minutes or so if we have time left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We will finish the hearing with you, and the Prosecutor will start tomorrow, if Mr. Pusic has no questions to ask, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I meant, Your Honour. If I manage now, within 11 minutes, to succeed in doing what I intended to do, then I'd have about 10 minutes left until the end of today's session. I would appreciate it if it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps 10 minutes will be taken up with questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Your Honours, I certainly won't have time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, now we are going to reorganise the documents and I'm going to ask you something that is relatively towards the end. But you can concentrate on my questions. Today, the Defence of Mr. Coric put some questions to you about one of your documents, and I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear Ms. Alaburic. There are other microphones on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Document P3238, your report to the Military Police Administration. The date is the 6th of July, 1993, and you mention Colonel Obradovic's order. Do you remember that question? I'm just asking you now whether you remember that answer. Please focus on me and what I'm saying to you, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you can also rely on e-court. It will only be faster for you. P3201, could we have that now, please, 3201. My question, Mr. Vidovic, is whether this is Nedjeljko Obradovic's order, the one that your question pertained to? Nedjeljko Obradovic, on the 5th of July, 1993, issues this order not to release anyone from prison without his personal signature, and he is sending that to the wardens of the prisons of Gabela, Dretelj, Heliodrom, and Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the date, can you give me the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, then that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P3220, could we have that document now, please. On the 6th of July, you are asking the Military Police Administration for further instructions in relation to the order of Nedjeljko Obradovic, which is document P3238. So now we have the document in e-court. This is the response: On the 6th of July, 1993, and Nedjeljko Obradovic is herein being told that it is the Military Police Administration that has sole jurisdiction over military or remand prisons, so therefore you're not authorised to issue orders regarding the release of prisoners. Paragraph 2 cancels the order of Nedjeljko Obradovic. Paragraph 3 says that all prisoners who are in military remand prisons and who were captured by the 1st Brigade of the HVO will, if they are released, be released only with the agreement of Nedjeljko Obradovic. And this document was sent to the same detention centres, Gabela, Dretelj, Heliodrom, and Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I think it would be useful, since my learned colleague linked up the two, could we look at the document stamp of 3238 to see when it was received, when this information from Mr. Vidovic was received? I mean, I did not understand what this was supposed to respond to. So if she is saying that this is Mr. Vidovic responding to Mr. Coric, let us look at the stamp and see when it was that Mr. Coric received this information from Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suggest that my colleague deals with all of this in the redirect, whatever she considers relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, did you receive this information from the Military Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it just now. 3220, that's the number; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three things in relation to this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, just tell me, did you receive this information or not? I'm not interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, now I'm going to read what Josip Praljak, a witness here, said in relation to this. 14943 is the transcript page. This is what he said. I shall quote it in English, because the transcript is in English: [In English] "And I remember, after that, that this order was conveyed to Stanko Bozic, and he was told that it was not meritorious and that we came under the authority -- we, the prison, came under the authority of the military police." [Interpretation] My question for you, Mr. Vidovic, is as follows: Did you personally ever see any order from Nedjeljko Obradovic later that pertained to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll just have to tell me what "later" refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After this date that we are talking about, the 6th of January, 19 -- the 6th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th of July, 1993, after that? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to go back to the subject of Mostar. P1654 is the document I'd like to deal with now. This is a report on the work of the military police and the security situation in the area of Mostar, and the chief of the Military Police Administration sent it to Mate Boban and to the head of the Defence Department on the 12th of March, 1993.
